content: Andrographis paniculata is a herbaceous plant belonging to the family Acanthaceae, native to India and Sri Lanka. It is extensively cultivated in southern Asia and has been traditionally used to treat infections and various diseases, particularly before the advent of antibiotics. The leaves and roots of the plant are primarily utilized for medicinal purposes. Scientific research on this herb has been ongoing for nearly three decades. Andrographis paniculata, also known as Kalmegh in Ayurveda, is an erect annual herb characterized by its extremely bitter taste, which is present in every part of the plant. In northeastern India, it is referred to as Maha-tita, meaning king of bitters, and is known by various vernacular names. It is also called Bhui-neem due to its resemblance in appearance and bitter taste to the Neem tree (Azadirachta indica), although it is much smaller in size. In Malaysia, it is known as Hempedu Bumi, which translates to bile of the earth, reflecting its intense bitterness and its use in traditional medicine. The genus Andrographis comprises 28 species of small annual shrubs distributed across tropical Asia, with only a few species being medicinally significant, among which Andrographis paniculata is the most prominent. The plant grows erect to a height of 30–110 cm in moist, shady areas. It has smooth leaves and white flowers with rose-purple spots on the petals. The seeds are numerous, sub-quadrate, and yellowish-brown. Since ancient times, Andrographis paniculata has been regarded as a wonder drug in traditional Siddha and Ayurvedic medicine systems, as well as in tribal medicine in India and other countries, for a wide range of clinical applications. Its therapeutic value is attributed to its mechanism of action, which likely involves enzyme induction. Extracts of the plant exhibit antityphoid and antifungal activities. Additionally, Kalmegh is reported to possess antihepatotoxic, antibiotic, antimalarial, antihepatitic, antithrombogenic, anti-inflammatory, antivenom, and antipyretic properties. It is also widely used as an immunostimulant agent. Recent studies at Bastyr University have confirmed the anti-HIV activity of andrographolide, a key compound extracted from the plant. Andrographis paniculata is distributed across tropical Asian countries, often in isolated patches. It thrives in diverse habitats, including plains, hill slopes, wastelands, farms, dry or wet lands, seashores, and even roadsides. Native populations of the plant are widespread in southern India and Sri Lanka, which are considered the center of origin and diversity for this species. The herb is also found in northern India, Java, Malaysia, Indonesia, the West Indies, and parts of the Americas, where it is likely introduced. It is also present in regions such as Hong Kong, Penang, Malacca, Pangkor Island, Malaya, Thailand, West Java, Borneo, Celebes, Brunei, Jamaica, Barbados, and the Bahamas. However, precise data on its introduction and naturalization in these areas are lacking. Unlike other species in the genus, Andrographis paniculata is commonly found in various regions of India, including plains and hilly areas up to 500 meters in altitude, which accounts for its widespread use. For centuries, rural and ethnic communities in India have used this herb to treat a variety of ailments. Andrographolide, the primary active constituent extracted from the leaves of the plant, is a bitter, water-soluble lactone. It has demonstrated protective effects in experimental models of carbon tetrachloride-induced liver damage in rats. This bitter compound was first isolated in pure form by Gorter in 1911. Andrographolide is also associated with liver protection under various experimental conditions, such as treatment with galactosamine and paracetamol. The hepatoprotective action of andrographolide is linked to the activity of specific metabolic enzymes. The pharmacological properties of Andrographis paniculata are diverse. Andrographolide, the major constituent of the plant extract, is responsible for many of its pharmacological activities. Studies have investigated the cellular processes and targets modulated by andrographolide treatment in human cancer and immune cells. Andrographolide has been shown to inhibit the in vitro proliferation of various tumor cell lines, representing different types of cancers. It exerts direct anticancer effects by inducing cell cycle arrest at the G0/G1 phase through the upregulation of the cell cycle inhibitory protein p27 and the downregulation of cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4). Its immunostimulatory activity is evidenced by increased lymphocyte proliferation and interleukin-2 production. Andrographolide also enhances tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) production and CD marker expression, leading to increased cytotoxic activity of lymphocytes against cancer cells, which may contribute to its indirect anticancer effects. The in vivo anticancer activity of andrographolide has been substantiated in models such as B16F0 melanoma syngeneic and HT29 xenograft systems. These findings suggest that andrographolide is a promising pharmacophore with anticancer and immunomodulatory activities, making it a potential candidate for development as a cancer therapeutic agent. The herb, commonly known as Kalmegh or green chiretta, is a well-known household remedy and forms the principal ingredient of a reputed household medicine (alui) used as a bitter tonic and febrifuge.
